concept.name: Treasury bill
concept.definition: A short-term U.S. Treasury marketable security with terms from 4 weeks up to 52 weeks. Bills are sold at face value or at a discount from face value and pay no periodic interest; the investor is paid the face value at maturity.
concept.intuition: A T-bill is a short-term loan to the U.S. government where the interest is built into the discount: you pay a bit less than face value now and collect the full face value in a few weeks or months.
concept.mechanics: Bills are auctioned regularly as zero-coupon-style discount instruments and quoted on a bank-discount basis. The return is the difference between purchase price and face value, and because maturities are under a year, price sensitivity to rate moves is small; bills are a core money-market and cash-management instrument.
concept.formula: Bank discount yield = ((face value - purchase price) / face value) x (360 / days to maturity).
concept.failure_modes: The main exposures are reinvestment risk (proceeds may roll into lower rates) and inflation risk. In extreme flight-to-quality episodes, bill yields can approach or fall below zero.
concept.misconceptions: That T-bills pay coupons like notes and bonds — they are discount instruments with a single payment at maturity. Also, the bank discount yield understates the true annualized return because it uses face value and a 360-day year.
concept.example: An investor buys a 26-week bill for $9,900 and receives $10,000 at maturity; the $100 difference is the interest.
